items.rationale:
- Workflow: code decides the next step. Agent: the model decides it.
- a: workflows use tools too (M7, tools make an agent).
- b: both designs use a model (M8, a workflow has no model).
- d: call count follows from who decides; it is not the test (M11).

- Code owns the loop: it runs the check, decides to retry and sets the cap of 3. That makes it a workflow.
- a: a loop alone does not make an agent; what matters is who controls it (M14).
- c: the model writes content, but does not choose the steps (M13).
- d: the design is not split; code decides every step here (M10).

- Booking has known steps in the same order every time, so code can run them: cheaper, faster, more predictable.
- a, b, c: the next step depends on what the last one returned, or on open-ended input, which is where an agent pays off.

- A fixed workflow only handles paths written into the code; you give up flexibility for unanticipated requests.
- b, c: a workflow can use tools and a model (M7, M8).
- d: predictable cost is what you gain, not lose (M9, agent is always the better choice).

items.answer: When the steps cannot be known in advance, because what to do next depends on what earlier steps return.
accepted: when the steps are unpredictable and depend on intermediate results
when the number and order of steps cannot be known ahead of time
when the steps can't be fixed in advance
when the task is open-ended and the model has to decide the steps
when the next step depends on what the last step returned
when the path depends on intermediate results
items.rationale:
- If steps are known up front, code can run them in a workflow.
- An agent earns its extra cost only when the path depends on results as they come in.
- 'The task is hard' or 'it needs tools' misses this; a workflow can do both.

- Control flow can be split: the code rule fixes the order of those two tools; the model still chooses everything else.
- a: the rule now overrides the model for that ordering (M13).
- b: one rule does not make every step code-decided (M10).
- d: mixing is normal; the two are ends of a spectrum (M10).
